subject: Engineering Fundamentals
title: Life Support: Engineering Air in a Sealed Box
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on Life Support: Engineering Air in a Sealed Box.

hook.text: The International Space Station recycles 93% of its water. Astronaut sweat, breath, and urine become tomorrow's drinking water.

buildup.text: CO2 must be scrubbed continuously. On the ISS, the Sabatier system combines CO2 with hydrogen to produce water and methane.

discovery.text: Oxygen comes from electrolysis — splitting water into hydrogen and oxygen using electricity from the station's solar panels.

twist.text: Apollo 13's CO2 scrubbers were the wrong shape for the lunar module. Engineers improvised a fix using duct tape and cardboard.

climax.text: Mars missions will need closed-loop life support for years. No resupply, no rescue, and every gram of air counts.

punchline.text: Recycle everything. Waste nothing. In space, your breath is tomorrow's oxygen.

quiz.question: How does the ISS produce oxygen for astronauts?
options: Compressed oxygen tanks are delivered on each resupply mission
Electrolysis splits recycled water into hydrogen and oxygen using solar power
Plants grown in the station's greenhouse produce all the required oxygen
